    A random gap.

docs.title: standard_PolynomialLFlangeSegment_sampler
docs.text:
standard_PolynomialLFlangeSegment_sampler(a, b, s, t, R, central_angle, Zg, bolt, Do, washer, nut, preload_sampler, ppl_sampler, dft_sampler, gap_sampler, tilt_sampler=lognorm_sampler(0.1 * deg, 0.5), E=210000000000.0, G=80770000000.0, s_ratio=1.0, r=0.01, k_shell='interp', settlement_factor=1.0, segment_class=None)

A sampler that yields random pyflange PolynomialLFlangeSegment objects.

For each realization, a random gap and a random flange tilt are drawn, and the bolt preload is sampled and averaged over the bolts affected by the gap (half of the bolts subtended by the gap angle, at least one), to account for the larger preload scatter at small gap angles (ref. [5], sections 4.4 and 6.4.1). The returned segment already includes the effect of the sampled preload losses (settlement and plastic), so its PPL and DFT attributes are zero.

The stochastic model of ref. [5], section 6.4 suggests a plastic loss with mean 0.03 and standard deviation 0.01 (norm_sampler(0.03, 1/3)), a dry film thickness with mean 250 µm and standard deviation 30 µm (norm_sampler(250e-6, 0.12)) and an inside flange inclination LN(0.1°, 0.5) (the default tilt_sampler).

Parameters:

  • a (float) –

    Distance between inner face of the flange and center of the bolt hole.

  • b (float) –

    Distance between center of the bolt hole and center-line of the shell.

  • s (float) –

    Shell thickness.

  • t (float) –

    Flange thickness.

  • R (float) –

    Shell outer curvature radius.

  • central_angle (float) –

    Angle subtended by the flange segment.

  • Zg (float) –

    Load applied to the flange segment shell at rest (normally dead weight of tower + RNA, divided by the number of bolts). Negative if compression.

  • bolt (Bolt) –

    Bolt object representing the flange segment bolt.

  • Do (float) –

    Bolt hole diameter.

  • washer (Washer) –

    Bolt washer.

  • nut (Nut) –

    Bolt nut.

  • preload_sampler (Generator) –

    Random preload sampler.

  • ppl_sampler (Generator) –

    Sampler of the percentage of pretension losses due to plastic deformation (non-dimensional, e.g. 0.03 for 3%).

  • dft_sampler (Generator) –

    Dry film thickness sampler.

  • gap_sampler (Generator) –

    Sampler of pyflange.flangesegments.Gap objects, such as standard_gap_sampler.

  • tilt_sampler (Generator, default: lognorm_sampler(0.1 * deg, 0.5) ) –

    Random tilt angle sampler. Sampled angles are reduced to the interval [0, pi]. Defaults to lognorm_sampler(0.1*deg, 0.50).

  • E (float, default: 210000000000.0 ) –

    Young modulus of the flange. Defaults to 210e9.

  • G (float, default: 80770000000.0 ) –

    Shear modulus of the flange. Defaults to 80.77e9.

  • s_ratio (float, default: 1.0 ) –

    Ratio of bottom shell thickness over s. Defaults to 1.0.

  • r (float, default: 0.01 ) –

    Rounding between flange and shell. Defaults to 0.01.

  • k_shell (str | float | None, default: 'interp' ) –

    Custom shell stiffness. If 'interp' (default), the stiffness is interpolated from the tabulated FEA results, as a function of the gap angle (see pyflange.flangesegments.shell_stiffness). If a number, it's used as the stiffness. If None, a simplified formula is used.

  • settlement_factor (float, default: 1.0 ) –

    Factor reducing the amount of bolt settlement, to be taken as 1.0 for torque tightening and 0.5 for tension tightening. If omitted, it defaults to 1.0.

  • segment_class (type, default: None ) –

    The class of the generated flange segments: PolynomialLFlangeSegment or one of its subclasses, such as PolynomialLFlangeSegmentED2. If omitted, it defaults to PolynomialLFlangeSegment.

Yields:

  • PolynomialLFlangeSegment –

    A random L-Flange segment object.

Example

The following example creates a L-Flange segment sampler and generates three random flange segments.

from math import pi
from metrum.units import mm, um, kN, deg

import pyflange.stats as stats
from pyflange.bolts import StandardMetricBolt, RoundNut
N_BOLTS = 156

fseg_samp = standard_PolynomialLFlangeSegment_sampler (
        a = 150*mm,        # distance between inner face of the flange and center of the bolt hole
        b = 122*mm,        # distance between center of the bolt hole and center-line of the shell
        s =  54*mm,        # shell thickness
        t = 172*mm,        # flange thickness
        R = 4000*mm,       # shell outer curvature radius
        central_angle = 2*pi / N_BOLTS,  # angle subtended by the flange segment

        Zg = -18044*kN / N_BOLTS,      # load applied to the flange segment shell at rest

        # Bolt object representing the flange segment bolt
        bolt = StandardMetricBolt("M80", "10.9", shank_length=160*mm,
                shank_diameter_ratio=76.1/80, stud=True),

        Do = 86*mm,               # Bolt hole diameter
        washer = None,            # Bolt washer
        nut = RoundNut("M80"),    # Bolt nut

        # bolt preload random sampler and preload losses parameters
        preload_sampler = stats.norm_sampler(2932.24*kN, 0.03), 
        ppl_sampler = stats.norm_sampler(0.03, 1/3),
        dft_sampler = stats.norm_sampler(250*um, 0.12),

        # gap object random sampler
        gap_sampler = stats.standard_gap_sampler(
                    flange_diameter = 8000*mm,
                    flange_flatness_tolerance = 0.0014,   # 1.4 mm/m
                    gap_angle_sampler = stats.lognorm_sampler(100*deg, 1.0),
                    gap_shape_factor_sampler = stats.norm_sampler(1.0, 0.15)
                ),

        s_ratio = 1.0,              # Ratio of bottom shell thickness over s.
        settlement_factor = 0.50    # Settlement reduction for tension tightening.
    )

fseg1 = next(fseg_samp)     # A random L-Flange segment object
fseg2 = next(fseg_samp)     # Another random L-Flange segment object
fseg3 = next(fseg_samp)     # Yet another random L-Flange segment object

docs.title: standard_markov_matrix_sampler
docs.text:
standard_markov_matrix_sampler(markov_matrix, mean_range_coeff=1.0, range_CoV=0.12)

Sampler that generates a random Markov matrix.

Each realization has the same cycles, means and duration as the design Markov matrix, while its ranges are scaled by a single log-normally distributed coefficient: the fatigue load factor X_FLS of the stochastic model of refs. [1] (Table 7) and [5] (section 6.3.1 and Table 8), with mean 1.0 and CoV 0.12. As explained in ref. [5], section 6.3.1, only the load ranges are scaled, not the mean values.

Parameters:

  • markov_matrix (MarkovMatrix) –

    The deterministic design Markov matrix.

  • mean_range_coeff (float, default: 1.0 ) –

    The mean value of the coefficient multiplying the load ranges of markov_matrix, assumed log-normally distributed. Defaults to 1.0.

  • range_CoV (float, default: 0.12 ) –

    The coefficient of variation of the coefficient multiplying the load ranges. Defaults to 0.12.

Yields:

  • MarkovMatrix –

    A random Markov matrix.

docs.title: standard_bolt_fatigue_curve_sampler
docs.text:
standard_bolt_fatigue_curve_sampler(bolt_nominal_diameter, mean_stress_factor=1.0, stress_factor_CoV=0.1, DS_ref_mean=62 * MPa)

Sampler that generates random bolt S-N curves.

The reference stress range of each curve is the product of DS_ref_mean and a normally distributed random coefficient: with the default values, this is the variable X_FAT ~ N(62 MPa, 0.10) of the stochastic model of refs. [1] (Table 7) and [5] (Table 8). The curves have the slopes, knee point and size effect of pyflange.fatigue.BoltFatigueCurve and no material safety factor (gamma_M = 1.0).

Parameters:

  • bolt_nominal_diameter (float) –

    The nominal diameter of the bolt, in meters.

  • mean_stress_factor (float, default: 1.0 ) –

    The mean value of the fatigue class coefficient, assumed normally distributed. Defaults to 1.

  • stress_factor_CoV (float, default: 0.1 ) –

    The coefficient of variation of the fatigue class coefficient, assumed normally distributed. Defaults to 0.10.

  • DS_ref_mean (float, default: 62 * MPa ) –

    The mean value of the fatigue curve reference stress range. If unknown it could be calculated as 1.24 times the fatigue class. If omitted, it defaults to 62 MPa.

Yields:

  • BoltFatigueCurve –

    A random bolt fatigue curve object.

docs.title: fatigue_case_sampler
docs.text:
fatigue_case_sampler(fseg_samp, markov_matrix_samp, fatigue_curve_samp, allowable_damage_samp, SMF=1.0)

Sampler that generates random fatigue cases.

Each realization combines one realization of each of the given samplers. The stochastic model of refs. [1] and [5] uses a log-normal allowable damage (Miner's rule model uncertainty) with mean 1.0 and CoV 0.30, e.g. lognorm_sampler(1.0, 0.30).

Parameters:

  • fseg_samp (Generator) –

    A pyflange.flangesegments.FlangeSegment sampler, such as standard_PolynomialLFlangeSegment_sampler.

  • markov_matrix_samp (Generator) –

    A pyflange.fatigue.MarkovMatrix sampler.

  • fatigue_curve_samp (Generator) –

    A pyflange.fatigue.BoltFatigueCurve sampler.

  • allowable_damage_samp (Generator) –

    A float sampler that generates random allowable damages.

  • SMF (float | Generator, default: 1.0 ) –

    Stress Multiplication Factor. If it is a sampler, a new SMF will be generated for every next fatigue case. If it is a float, it will be applied to every next fatigue case. If omitted, it defaults to 1.0.

Yields:

  • BoltFatigueAnalysis –

    A random BoltFatigueAnalysis object.

docs.title: pyflange.utils
docs.text:
Internal utilities shared by the other PyFlange modules.

This module collects small helpers that are used throughout the library:

  • Logger, a logger configured with the PyFlange logging level.
  • load_csv_database, which loads the tabular data (bolt dimensions, material properties, shell stiffness results, etc.) shipped with the package.
  • reduce_to_pi, an angle reduction function.

These helpers are mainly meant for internal use, but they are public and documented because they may be useful when extending the library.

Functions:

  • Logger –

    Create a logger configured with the PyFlange logging level.

  • load_csv_database –

    Load one of the CSV databases shipped with the package.

  • reduce_to_pi –

    Reduce an angle to the interval [0, pi].

docs.title: reduce_to_pi
docs.text:
reduce_to_pi(angle)

Reduce an angle to the interval [0, pi].

The angle is first wrapped to (-pi, pi] and then its absolute value is taken. This is useful for angles whose sign is irrelevant, such as a tilt angle magnitude.

Parameters:

  • angle (float) –

    The angle, in radians.

Returns:

  • float –

    The equivalent non-negative angle in radians, between 0 and pi.

Example 
from math import pi
reduce_to_pi(3*pi/2)    # pi/2
reduce_to_pi(-0.3)      # 0.3

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
These pages take you from a Windows computer without Python to your first flange fatigue analysis. No programming experience is needed: every command is given in full, and every step tells you what you should see.

There are two ways of using PyFlange:

  • Without writing code

    Describe the flange in a text file (a case file) and run the analysis with one command. Results are written to JSON, CSV or Excel files.

    Good for routine checks and for Monte Carlo simulations of a single flange.

  • With Python scripts

    Build the flange model in a short Python script. You have access to every intermediate quantity and you can run parameter studies, plots and batches.

    Good for design iterations and for anything the command line does not cover (for example T-flanges).

Both ways use the same model and give the same results.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
1. Install PyFlange: install Python, open a terminal and install the package. About 10 minutes.
  2. First analysis without code: download an example case file, run a fatigue analysis and open the results in Excel.
  3. First Python script: write, run and modify a short script that computes a bolt force curve.

When you are done, continue with the tutorials.

Already familiar with Python?

Install the package with pip install pyflange and go straight to the tutorials.

docs.title: First analysis without code
docs.text: In this step you run a deterministic bolt fatigue analysis of an example L-flange, using the PyFlange command-line tool. You need PyFlange installed.

docs.title: 1. Create a working folder
docs.text:
Open a terminal (Win, type cmd, Enter) and create a folder for your analyses:

C:\Users\yourname>mkdir flange-analyses
C:\Users\yourname>cd flange-analyses
C:\Users\yourname\flange-analyses>

docs.title: 2. Download the example case
docs.text:
Download the example case file fatigue-case.json and save it in the flange-analyses folder. (In most browsers: right-click the link, Save link as....)

Check that the file is there:

C:\Users\yourname\flange-analyses>dir
...
23/10/2026  10:15             3.512 fatigue-case.json

Look inside the case file

A case file is a plain text file. Open it with Notepad (notepad fatigue-case.json) or, better, with an editor such as VS Code or Notepad++, which highlight the structure. It describes an L-flange of an 8 m tower with 156 M80 bolts, a 30° design gap, a 30-year load spectrum and the bolt S-N curve. All values are in SI units (m, N, Pa, rad). Every field is explained in the JSON format reference.

docs.title: 3. Run the analysis
docs.text:
C:\Users\yourname\flange-analyses>py -m pyflange determ fatigue-case.json --xlsx
Performing deterministic fatigue analysis for case 'fatigue-case.json' ...
... loading data from 'fatigue-case.json'
... building the model
... writing data to json file '.\fatigue-case-res.json'
... writing data to excel file '.\fatigue-case-res.xlsx'
... DONE!

determ stands for deterministic. The --xlsx option also writes the results to an Excel file.

docs.title: 4. Look at the results
docs.text:
Open the Excel file:

C:\Users\yourname\flange-analyses>start fatigue-case-res.xlsx

The sheet is a two-column table of all the inputs and results. The most important rows are:

Key Value Meaning damage 0.501 Miner's sum of the bolt for the load spectrum. FatigueLife 59.8 Fatigue life, in the same unit as the Markov matrix duration (years). FlangeSegment.BoltPreload 2733846 Bolt preload after settlement and plastic losses, in N. FlangeSegment.Point1.Z ... Point4.Fs The points of the bolt force polynomial (see Model overview). FlangeSegment.TransferFunctions.Z, .Fs, .Ms The bolt force and moment curves, as lists of 100 values.

Each value cell has an Excel name equal to its key, so you can refer to it from another workbook, e.g. ='fatigue-case-res.xlsx'!damage.

The damage is lower than the allowable damage of 1.0: the bolts of this flange pass the fatigue check for the 30° gap.

docs.title: 5. Try another gap
docs.text:
IEC 61400-6 requires the gap angles 30°, 60°, 90° and 120° to be checked. Run the same case with a 90° gap of 2.75 mm, the AMD1 design gap height for this tower diameter:

C:\Users\yourname\flange-analyses>py -m pyflange determ fatigue-case.json --gap-angle 90 --gap-height 2.75

The result is written to fatigue-case-res-GapA90.0deg-gaph2.75mm.json. Open it with Notepad and look for "damage": it is larger than 1, so the 90° gap governs and the bolts fail the check. The design gaps tutorial shows how to run this check systematically.

docs.title: What you have learned
docs.text:
• A flange case is described in a JSON file.
  • py -m pyflange determ CASE.json runs the deterministic analysis, and the gap and tilt can be changed from the command line.
  • The command-line reference lists all the commands, including the Monte Carlo simulation (sample).

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Write your first Python script

docs.title: First Python script
docs.text: In this step you write a short Python script that builds an L-flange segment and prints its bolt force curve. You need PyFlange installed.

docs.title: 1. Open IDLE
docs.text:
Python comes with a simple editor called IDLE. Press Win, type idle and press Enter. A window titled IDLE Shell opens.

Other editors

For larger projects, Visual Studio Code with the Python extension is a better editor. Everything on this page works the same way there: write the script, save it, run it.

docs.title: 2. Write the script
docs.text:
In IDLE, choose File > New File. An empty editor window opens. Copy the following script into it (use the copy button at the top-right of the box):

first_script.py
from math import pi
from pyflange.bolts import StandardMetricBolt, RoundNut
from pyflange.flangesegments import PolynomialLFlangeSegment, Gap

# Units: meters, newtons, radians
mm = 0.001
kN = 1000
deg = pi/180

# The flange segment: one bolt of an L-flange with 156 M80 bolts
fseg = PolynomialLFlangeSegment(
    a = 150*mm,                     # inner face of the flange to bolt axis
    b = 122*mm,                     # bolt axis to shell center line
    s = 54*mm,                      # shell thickness
    t = 172*mm,                     # flange thickness
    R = 4000*mm,                    # shell outer radius
    central_angle = 2*pi/156,       # 156 bolts
    Zg = -115*kN,                   # dead weight per bolt
    bolt = StandardMetricBolt("M80", "10.9", shank_length=160*mm, stud=True),
    Fv = 2876*kN,                   # bolt preload
    Do = 86*mm,                     # bolt hole diameter
    washer = None,
    nut = RoundNut("M80"),
    gap = Gap(height=0.89*mm, angle=30*deg))

# Print the bolt force for some values of the shell force
for Z in [-200*kN, 0*kN, 200*kN, 400*kN, 600*kN, 800*kN, 1000*kN]:
    Fs = fseg.bolt_axial_force(Z)
    print(f"Shell force {Z/kN:6.0f} kN  ->  bolt force {Fs/kN:7.1f} kN")

Choose File > Save As..., go to your flange-analyses folder and save the file as first_script.py.

docs.title: 3. Run it
docs.text:
Press F5 (or Run > Run Module). The output appears in the IDLE Shell window:

Shell force   -200 kN  ->  bolt force  2876.0 kN
Shell force      0 kN  ->  bolt force  2878.2 kN
Shell force    200 kN  ->  bolt force  2892.4 kN
Shell force    400 kN  ->  bolt force  2919.9 kN
Shell force    600 kN  ->  bolt force  2960.7 kN
Shell force    800 kN  ->  bolt force  3014.9 kN
Shell force   1000 kN  ->  bolt force  3082.3 kN

You can also run the script from the terminal:

C:\Users\yourname\flange-analyses>py first_script.py

docs.title: 4. Understand the script
docs.text:
• from ... import ... lines load the PyFlange objects used by the script: a standard bolt and nut, the L-flange segment model and the gap.
  • Units. PyFlange does not know about units: it expects all values in one consistent system. The script uses meters, newtons and radians, and defines mm, kN and deg so that you can write 150*mm instead of 0.150. See Units and conventions.
  • PolynomialLFlangeSegment(...) creates the model of one flange segment: the slice of the flange that contains one bolt. The symbols a, b, s, t follow IEC 61400-6 and are explained in the Nomenclature. Zg is the shell force per bolt due to the dead weight (negative: compression).
  • fseg.bolt_axial_force(Z) returns the bolt force for a shell force Z acting on the segment.
  • print(f"...") prints a line of text. The expressions between braces are replaced by their value; :7.1f means 7 characters wide, 1 decimal.

docs.title: 5. Change something
docs.text:
Try these changes one at a time. Save (Ctrl+S) and run (F5) after each one.

  • Make the gap larger: gap = Gap(height=2.0*mm, angle=30*deg). The bolt force grows faster with the shell force, because a larger part of the load goes through the bolt until the gap closes.
  • Reduce the preload: Fv = 2500*kN.
  • Print the bolt bending moment as well: add the line print(fseg.bolt_bending_moment(Z)) inside the for loop (indented like the other lines of the loop).
IndentationError or SyntaxError

Python uses indentation to group lines. The lines inside the for loop must be indented by the same number of spaces (4 in this script). A missing comma or parenthesis also causes a SyntaxError: the error message shows the line where Python got confused.

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pyflange'

PyFlange is not installed for the Python you are using. Run py -m pip install pyflange again, and check that IDLE was started from the same Python installation (py -m idlelib starts it).

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: You now know how to build a flange segment in Python. The L-flange tutorial continues from here: it checks the validity of the model, plots the bolt force and moment curves and performs the fatigue analysis.

docs.title: Install PyFlange
docs.text: This page explains how to install Python and PyFlange on Windows 10 or 11. You do not need administrator rights.

docs.title: 1. Install Python
docs.text:
PyFlange needs Python 3.9 or later. If you are not sure whether Python is already installed, skip to step 3: if the check works, you can skip the installation.

  1. Go to https://www.python.org/downloads/ and click the yellow Download Python 3.x.x button.
  2. Run the downloaded file (python-3.x.x-amd64.exe).
  3. In the first window of the installer:
    • tick Add python.exe to PATH at the bottom of the window;
    • click Install Now.
  4. Wait until the installer shows Setup was successful, then click Close.

Company computers

If your company installs software for you (e.g. through a software center), ask for Python 3.12 or later and check that the py command works as described in step 3.

docs.title: 2. Open a terminal
docs.text:
A terminal (also called command prompt) is a window where you type commands instead of clicking.

  1. Press the Win key, type cmd and press Enter.

  2. A black window opens, showing a line like:

    C:\Users\yourname>

    This is the prompt. It shows the current folder, here your user folder. You type a command after the > and press Enter to run it.

Windows Terminal and PowerShell

You can also use Windows Terminal or PowerShell. All the commands in this documentation work in all of them.

A few commands you will use:

Command What it does cd Documents Go to the Documents folder inside the current folder. cd .. Go up one folder. cd C:\Projects\flange Go to a specific folder. Use quotes if the path contains spaces: cd "C:\My Projects". mkdir flange Create a folder called flange. dir List the files in the current folder. start . Open the current folder in the File Explorer. cls Clear the window.

Press Up to recall the previous command, and Tab to complete a file or folder name.

docs.text:
In the terminal, type the following command and press Enter:

C:\Users\yourname>py --version
Python 3.12.7

'py' is not recognized as an internal or external command

Python is not installed, or it was installed without the py launcher. Run the installer again: choose Modify, make sure py launcher is selected and complete the installation. Then close the terminal and open a new one: a terminal only sees programs that were installed before it was opened.

The Microsoft Store opens

Windows has a shortcut that opens the Store when you type python. Use py instead of python, as in this documentation, or install Python from python.org as described above.

docs.title: 4. Install PyFlange
docs.text:
Type:

C:\Users\yourname>py -m pip install pyflange

pip is the Python package installer. It downloads PyFlange and the packages it needs (numpy, scipy, pandas, ...). After a few seconds to a few minutes, the last line should be:

Successfully installed ... pyflange-x.y.z ...

Behind a company proxy

If pip cannot connect to the internet, ask your IT department for the proxy address and use: py -m pip install --proxy http://proxy.company.com:8080 pyflange

C:\Users\yourname>py -m pyflange --version
pyflange x.y.z

docs.title: Modelling
docs.text:
ValueError: Failure mode D detected, while only failure mode B is supported

validate() found that the flange fails at ULS in a mode for which the polynomial model is not valid (see Validity of the model). Typically the flange is too thin compared with the bolt (mode D or E) or the shell is too weak. Change the geometry, or use FEA.

Which shell stiffness should I use?

By default (k_shell=None) the simplified formula of ref. [2], eq. G.43 is used, which is conservative. A better estimate is the FEA database of ref. [5], 9.3.1: pass k_shell=shell_stiffness(R, s, gap_angle), or "k_shell": "interp" in a JSON case. The database covers diameters of 3 to 10 m, shell thicknesses of 10 to 150 mm and gap angles of 10° to 180°; outside this range shell_stiffness returns nan.

Is Fv the preload before or after losses?

Before losses. The model subtracts the settlement and plastic losses defined by DFT, settlement_factor and PPL; the result is fseg.bolt_preload. If your preload already includes all the losses, leave PPL and DFT at zero. Note that the coefficient of variation term of ref. [2], eq. (23) is not applied by PyFlange: include it in Fv.

Why does the bolt force differ from my FEA results?

The polynomial model is an approximation calibrated on FEA results (refs. [1] and [5]), so some difference is expected; the stress multiplication factor of ref. [5], 6.5 accounts for this model uncertainty. First check that the gap, the shell stiffness, the inclination and the preload are the same in both models.

Can I model T-flanges in a JSON case file?

Not yet: the JSON format and the command line support L-flanges only. Use the Python API, see the T-flange tutorial.

Should I use the AMD1 or the ED2 classes?

IEC 61400-6:2020+AMD1:2025 is the published standard: use the AMD1 classes (PolynomialLFlangeSegment, PolynomialTFlangeSegment) for design. The ED2 classes implement a draft and are useful to anticipate the effect of the next edition.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
The damage is zero or extremely small

The bolt force increases significantly only when the shell force approaches the gap opening region. Check that the Markov matrix contains tower bending moments in N·m (not kN·m or stresses), and that Zg is the dead weight per bolt (per bolt pair for T-flanges), in N.

The damage is nan

Usually an input is nan, for example k_shell from shell_stiffness outside the range of the FEA database. Check the intermediate quantities with pyflange determ, or print fseg.shell_force_at_tensile_ULS and the other points.

The Monte Carlo results change at every run

Use --seed on the command line, or numpy.random.seed(...) in Python.

docs.title: Model overview
docs.text: This page summarizes the model implemented by PyFlange and tells where each part is found in the code and in the references. It is not a substitute for IEC 61400-6 Annex G (ref. [2]) and its background documents (refs. [1] and [5]), which give the full derivation.

docs.title: The flange segment
docs.text:
The flange is divided into segments, each containing one bolt (L-flange) or one pair of bolts (T-flange). A segment is loaded by the meridional shell force Z, positive in tension. In the unloaded state the segment carries the dead weight Zg (negative) and the bolt carries its preload. The geometric parameters are shown in the Nomenclature.

A gap between the two flanges, caused by flatness imperfections, is described by its height, its angle and its shape (Gap). Before the flanges are in full contact, part of the external load is needed to close the gap, which makes the bolt force increase faster than in a perfect flange.

docs.title: Bolt force curve
docs.text:
The bolt force FS(Z) is defined by four points (ref. [2], Table G.1):

Point Meaning PyFlange property P1 Flange at rest: Z1 = dead weight, FS,1 = preload after losses shell_force_at_rest, bolt_force_at_rest P2 Ultimate tensile state shell_force_at_tensile_ULS, bolt_force_at_tensile_ULS P3 Small displacement: sets the initial slope of the curve shell_force_at_small_displacement, bolt_force_at_small_displacement P4 Gap completely closed shell_force_at_closed_gap
  • For Z ≥ Z1, FS is the quadratic polynomial through P1, P2 and P3 (ref. [2], eq. G.32).
  • For Z4 < Z < Z1, it is a quadratic polynomial with the same slope at P1 and zero slope at P4.
  • For Z ≤ Z4, it is constant.

The main ingredients of the points are:

  • Preload after losses (ref. [2], 6.7.5.1): the preload Fv reduced by settlement (eqs. (27), (28)) and plastic strain (eq. (24)). Property bolt_preload.
  • Lever ratio and a' (ref. [2], G.1.3; ref. [6]): the effective inner lever arm of an L-flange, with the action point correction of Tobinaga and Ishihara.
  • Gap stiffness (ref. [2], eqs. G.41 to G.46): the shell stiffness kshell (simplified formula G.43, a value given by the user, or the FEA database of shell_stiffness) plus the flange bending stiffness kfl.
  • Gap closing force ΔZgap (ref. [2], eqs. G.39, G.40), reduced by the flange inclination (ref. [2], G.2.4, eqs. G.66 to G.70) and, for T-flanges, increased by early prying (eqs. G.47, G.48).
  • Stiffness correction factor αk (ref. [2], eqs. G.49 to G.52), which scales Z2 and Z3.
  • The gap shape factor scales FS,2 − FS,1 and the initial slope, to represent gaps that are not sinusoidal (used in Monte Carlo simulations).

The values of all intermediate quantities are reported by pyflange determ (see JSON result files).

docs.title: Bolt bending moment
docs.text: The bolt moment MS(Z) is computed from the rotation of the flange at the bolt (ref. [2], G.2.3): eqs. G.59 and G.60 for L-flanges, which give a quadratic curve in Z, and eqs. G.61 to G.63 for T-flanges, which give a cubic curve. The compressive branch is built as for the bolt force.

docs.title: Validity of the model
docs.text:
The polynomial model is valid only when the flange fails in the intended mode at the ultimate limit state (ref. [2], G.1.2 and G.2.1):

  • L-flanges: failure mode B (bolt failure with plastic hinges in the flange and shell, eq. G.30);
  • T-flanges: failure mode A (bolt failure, eq. G.31).

failure_mode(fy_sh, fy_fl) computes the ultimate shell force of the modes A, B, D and E and returns the governing one; validate(fy_sh, fy_fl) raises an error if it is not the required mode. PyFlange does not call validate automatically: call it in your scripts.

Other limits of the model, given in ref. [2], are not checked by PyFlange, for example the flatness tolerance of 1.4 mm/m for the analytical design gap (6.7.5.2) and the conditions for the simplified plastic preload loss (6.7.5.1.3, 6.7.5.1.4).

docs.title: Fatigue damage
docs.text:
The bolt stress range is the axial stress range plus the bending stress range reduced by κb (ref. [2], eqs. (42), (43)), on the bolt stress area. The S-N curve has detail category 50 MPa at 2·106 cycles, slopes 3 and 5, knee point at 2·106 cycles, size reduction ks (eq. (44)), γM = 1.1 and no endurance limit. The damage is the Miner's sum; the allowable damage is 1.0 (6.7.5.4).

The stress ranges can be multiplied by a stress multiplication factor (SMF), which represents the model uncertainty of the analytical model (ref. [5], 6.5).

docs.title: ED2
docs.text:
The changes proposed for IEC 61400-6 ED2 (ref. [5], section 9.7) are implemented in separate classes, which have the same interface as the AMD1 ones:

# Change L-flange T-flange 1 Torsional correction factor fk,gap on the gap closing force PolynomialLFlangeSegmentED2 not applicable 2 Gap stiffness: ftot applied to the shell stiffness only PolynomialLFlangeSegmentED2 PolynomialTFlangeSegmentED2 3 Lower bound of a* reduced from 0.4·a' to 0.3·a' PolynomialLFlangeSegmentED2 not applicable – Weibull gap height distribution, 75% design fractile (ref. [5], 2.2.4) gap_height_distribution_ED2 gap_height_distribution_ED2

docs.title: Monte Carlo simulation
docs.text: The probabilistic model of refs. [1] and [5] (section 6) treats preload, preload losses, gap, flange inclination, fatigue loads, S-N curve, Miner's rule and model uncertainty as random variables. PyFlange provides random samplers for each of them in pyflange.stats; the sample command and sample_fatiguecase combine them as described in the JSON format.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
Where PyFlange deviates from the text of ref. [2], it does so to reproduce the reference results it is validated against (see Validation), or because the standard leaves room for interpretation. The notable cases are:

  • ftot for small gap angles. For L-flanges, the gap stiffness factor ftot (eq. G.42) is further reduced by the factor min(αgap/30°, 1)², which only matters for gap angles below 30°, i.e. in Monte Carlo simulations.
  • Wall thickness. The segment width and the shell parameters use the mean of the upper and lower wall thickness (s_ratio).
  • Tower section modulus. The conversion from bending moment to shell force uses the section modulus at the shell mid-surface, which is slightly conservative.
  • Macro-geometric factor. In bolt_markov_matrix, the macro_geometric_factor (SCF of 6.7.5.3) is applied to the dead weight as well as to the mean and range values.
  • T-flange bolt moment. The tensile branch is the exact cubic of eq. G.61, while the SGRE reference workbooks fit a quadratic through three points (differences of about 1%).

docs.text: PyFlange names follow the symbols of IEC 61400-6 Annex G (ref. [2]) where possible. This page maps the parameters and properties of the flange segment classes to the symbols of the standard.

docs.text: PyFlange IEC 61400-6 Description MarkovMatrix.range, .mean, .cycles ΔM, Mmean, n Load bins. BoltFatigueCurve(diameter, DS_ref, gamma_M) d, ΔσC, γM Bolt S-N curve (ref. [2], 6.7.5.4). BoltFatigueAnalysis.damage D Miner's sum. BoltFatigueAnalysis.allowable_damage Dallow Allowable damage (1.0 in ref. [2]). SMF SMF Stress multiplication factor (model uncertainty, ref. [5], 6.5).

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
The Python API does not convert units: it computes with the numbers you give it. Use one consistent system for all inputs, and the results come out in the same system. The recommended system, used throughout this documentation and by the standard databases, is SI:

Quantity Unit Length m Force N Moment N·m Stress, elastic modulus Pa Angle rad Stiffness of the shell (k_shell) N/m per m of segment width (N/m²) Duration of a Markov matrix free (e.g. years); the fatigue life has the same unit

Standard bolts and the FEA database are in SI units

StandardMetricBolt, the nuts, washers and hole diameters, and shell_stiffness return values in m and Pa. If you use them, all other inputs must be in SI units too.

A convenient way to write readable input is to define unit factors:

from math import pi
mm, kN, MPa, deg = 0.001, 1000, 1e6, pi/180

t = 172*mm          # 0.172 m
Fv = 2876*kN        # 2 876 000 N
gap_angle = 30*deg  # 0.5236 rad

The JSON case format always uses SI units. The command line options --gap-angle, --gap-height and --tilt-angle are the only exceptions: they are given in degrees and millimeters for convenience.

docs.title: Sign conventions
docs.text:
• Shell force Z: positive in tension. The dead weight Zg is negative.
  • Gap closing forces (DZ_gap, DZ_gap_tot in the reports): negative values close the gap.
  • Flange inclination tilt_angle: positive values represent the inside inclination of the flange contact surface considered in ref. [2], G.2.4, which improves the bolt force curve (ref. [5], 6.4.2).
  • Bolt bending moment: positive under tensile shell forces. Only its range matters for the fatigue analysis.

docs.title: Shell force and bending moment
docs.text:
The flange segment models work with the shell force per segment. To get it from a tower bending moment M, PyFlange uses (ref. [2], eq. G.33):

\[Z = \frac{M}{W} \, s \, c\]

where W is the section modulus of the tower shell and s·c the shell cross-section area of the segment. This conversion is done by bolt_markov_matrix and by BoltFatigueAnalysis, which expect a Markov matrix of tower bending moments. To evaluate the transfer functions directly, pass the shell force per segment.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: PyFlange is verified against the reference implementation of the polynomial model by Siemens Gamesa (SGRE): a set of Excel workbooks that compute the model of IEC 61400-6 AMD1 step by step. The comparison is automated and runs as part of the test suite, so every change to the code is checked against the reference values.

docs.title: Validation cases
docs.text:
Case Flange Diameter Gap Tilt Shell stiffness L1 L, 120 × M80 7.5 m sinusoidal 0° interpolated / simplified L2 L, 120 × M80 7.5 m sinusoidal 0.25° interpolated / simplified L3 L, 120 × M80 7.5 m shape factor 1.2 0° interpolated / simplified L4 L 4.6 m sinusoidal 0° interpolated / simplified T5 T 7.5 m sinusoidal 0° interpolated / simplified T6 T 7.5 m shape factor 1.5 0° interpolated / simplified T7 T 7.5 m shape factor 1.5 1° interpolated / simplified T8 T 7.5 m sinusoidal 1° interpolated / simplified

Each case is computed for the gap angles 30°, 60°, 90° and 120°, with the AMD1 design gap heights. The 16 case files contain 3264 comparisons in total: the bolt and flange stiffnesses, the gap height distribution, the points and coefficients of the bolt force and moment polynomials, the gap closing forces and the fatigue damage.

A quantity passes when it differs from the reference value by less than 1%. For some quantities, each case file sets a larger tolerance, listed in its tolerances object:

  • the shell stiffness interpolated from the FEA database, and the gap stiffness and closing forces derived from it: up to 3%, mostly for the 30° gap, because the workbooks interpolate the database differently;
  • the fatigue damage: up to 5.5%, because it amplifies small differences of the bolt stress ranges;
  • the bolt moment curve of T-flanges (initial slope c_ini_M and closed-gap moment Ms_min): up to 7%, because the reference workbooks fit a quadratic where PyFlange uses the exact cubic (see below);
  • the slope of the bolt force polynomial at P1 (c_ini_true), a diagnostic quantity that is very sensitive to the polynomial coefficients: up to 30%, and more in two cases where the reference value is close to zero.

Run the validation with --failed and a lower --rtol to see these differences.

docs.title: Running the validation
docs.text:
The validation cases are in the validations folder of the source repository. After cloning it:

py validations/validate.py validations/references/L1-interp.json

Useful options:

Option Effect --failed Show only the comparisons that fail. --rtol 0.005 Use a different allowable mismatch. --excel Also write the results to copies of the SGRE workbooks in validations/results/ (requires Excel and xlwings).

To run all the cases: py validations/validate.py validations/references/*.json.

docs.title: Known differences
docs.text:
• The reference workbooks fit a quadratic polynomial through three points for the tensile bolt moment of T-flanges, while PyFlange evaluates the exact cubic of ref. [2], eq. G.61. The validation compares the quadratic coefficients of the workbooks with the quadratic through the PyFlange points.
  • The ED2 classes are not covered by the reference workbooks. They are tested against the formulas of ref. [5] in the unit tests.

docs.title: Unit tests
docs.text: Besides the validation, the test suite (py -m pytest) contains unit tests of every module, and runs the example scripts of the tutorials.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
Each tutorial is a complete, working example that you can download and run. The scripts are tested automatically against the current version of PyFlange, so the code on these pages always works.

Tutorial You will learn to Needs L-flange, deterministic Build an L-flange segment, check the validity of the model, plot the bolt force and moment curves, compute the fatigue damage. Python T-flange, deterministic The same for a T-flange, and the differences with L-flanges. Python Design gap angles and ED2 Check the four design gap angles of IEC 61400-6 and compare the AMD1 and ED2 models. Python Monte Carlo from the command line Run a probabilistic analysis of a JSON case, inspect the statistics and single realizations. Command line Monte Carlo in Python Build a custom Monte Carlo simulation with the random samplers of pyflange.stats. Python Writing case files from Python Create case variants, run batches and collect the results in Excel. Python

If you have never used Python, start with Getting started.

docs.title: Conventions used in the tutorials
docs.text:
• All values are in SI units (m, N, Pa, rad). The scripts define mm, kN, MPa and deg to make the input readable: 150*mm is 0.150 m.
  • The example flange is an L-flange of an 8 m monopile or tower with 156 M80 bolts. The values are realistic but do not belong to a real project.
  • The Markov matrices are invented for the examples. In a real assessment, they come from the load calculation of the turbine.
  • References such as ref. [2], eq. G.36 point to the documents on the References page.

Plots

Some tutorials draw plots with matplotlib, which is not installed together with PyFlange. Install it with py -m pip install matplotlib. The scripts work without it, they only skip the plots.

docs.title: Writing case files from Python
docs.text:
The JSON case files used by the command line can also be read, modified and written from Python with pyflange.io. This is convenient for running variants of a case and for collecting the results of many cases in one table.

Download the full script: case_file.py. Run it in a folder that contains fatigue-case.json.

docs.title: 1. Load a case
docs.text:
from pyflange.io import load_inputfile, create_fatiguecase

case = load_inputfile("fatigue-case.json")      # a plain Python dictionary
fcase = create_fatiguecase(case)                # a BoltFatigueAnalysis object
print(f"Damage of the example case: {fcase.damage:.3f}")

Damage of the example case: 0.501

load_inputfile returns the content of the file as a dictionary, with the same structure as the JSON file. create_fatiguecase builds the BoltFatigueAnalysis from it. To do both in one step, use load_fatiguecase.

docs.title: 2. Write variants of the case
docs.text:
Change the dictionary and save it with dict_to_json. Here we create one case per design gap angle, with the AMD1 design gap height of each angle:

import copy
from pyflange.io import dict_to_json
from pyflange.stats import gap_height_distribution

D = 2 * case["FlangeSegment"]["R"]          # tower outer diameter
u_tol = 0.0014                              # flatness tolerance, 1.4 mm/m

for angle_deg in (30, 60, 90, 120):
    angle = angle_deg * deg
    variant = copy.deepcopy(case)
    variant["CaseID"] = f"Example, {angle_deg} deg gap"
    variant["FlangeSegment"]["gap"]["angle"] = angle
    variant["FlangeSegment"]["gap"]["height"] = gap_height_distribution(D, u_tol, angle * D/2).ppf(0.95)
    dict_to_json(variant, f"case-gap{angle_deg}.json")
    print(f"Written case-gap{angle_deg}.json")

Since the example case has "k_shell": "interp", the shell stiffness is interpolated for the new gap angle when the case is loaded.

docs.title: 3. Export a case with its results
docs.text:
fatiguecase_to_dict converts an analysis back to the JSON format. With verbose=True it adds the results and the intermediate quantities of the model, like the output of pyflange determ:

from pyflange.io import fatiguecase_to_dict

result = fatiguecase_to_dict(fcase, verbose=True)   # input + results + report
dict_to_json(result, "case-res.json")
print(f"Fatigue life: {result['FatigueLife']:.1f} years")

The same function works for an analysis built in Python, for example the fatigue object of the L-flange tutorial: this is the way to create a case file from a Python model.

from pyflange.io import fatiguecase_to_dict, dict_to_json
dict_to_json(fatiguecase_to_dict(fatigue), "my-case.json")

Note

The JSON format currently supports L-flange segments only.

docs.title: 4. Run a batch
docs.text:
import glob
import pandas as pd
from pyflange.io import load_fatiguecase

rows = []
for path in sorted(glob.glob("case-gap*.json")):
    fc = load_fatiguecase(path)
    rows.append({"case": path,
                 "gap angle [deg]": fc.fseg.gap.angle / deg,
                 "damage": fc.damage,
                 "fatigue life [years]": fc.fatigue_life})

table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(table.to_string(index=False))
table.to_excel("results.xlsx", index=False)

case-gap120.json            120.0 1.080555             27.763512

The table is also saved to results.xlsx. To add a Monte Carlo simulation of each case, use sample_fatiguecase, which returns the same table as the sample command.

docs.title: Design gap angles and ED2
docs.text:
IEC 61400-6 does not prescribe a single design gap: the gap angles 30°, 60°, 90° and 120° are potentially design-driving, and the one giving the highest fatigue damage is decisive (ref. [2], 6.7.5.3). The design gap height depends on the gap angle. This tutorial runs the four cases for the flange of the L-flange tutorial, first with the AMD1 model and then with the model proposed for ED2.

Download the full script: design_gaps.py

docs.title: 1. Common parameters
docs.text:
All the parameters except the gap and the shell stiffness are the same for the four cases. We store them in a dictionary and pass it to the class with **common:

from pyflange.bolts import StandardMetricBolt, RoundNut, standard_hole_diameter
from pyflange.fatigue import MarkovMatrix, BoltFatigueAnalysis

D = 8000*mm                 # tower outer diameter
R = D/2
s = 54*mm
u_tol = 0.0014              # flatness tolerance, 1.4 mm/m
n_bolts = 156

# Parameters shared by all the flange segments of this study
common = dict(
    a = 150*mm, b = 122*mm, s = s, t = 172*mm, R = R,
    central_angle = 2*pi / n_bolts,
    Zg = -18044*kN / n_bolts,
    bolt = StandardMetricBolt("M80", "10.9", shank_length=160*mm,
                              shank_diameter_ratio="pitch", stud=True),
    Fv = 2876*kN,
    Do = standard_hole_diameter("M80"),
    washer = None,
    nut = RoundNut("M80"),
    tilt_angle = 0.1*deg,
    PPL = 0.05, DFT = 300e-6, settlement_factor = 0.5)

mkvm = MarkovMatrix(
    range  = np.array([ 25,  50, 100, 150, 200, 250,  300, 375, 500, 625]) * 1e6,
    mean   = np.array([100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 100,  100, 100, 100, 100]) * 1e6,
    cycles = np.array([3e8, 1e8, 3e7, 8e6, 2e6, 5e5, 1.5e5, 4e4, 8e3, 1e3]),
    duration = 30)

docs.title: 2. AMD1
docs.text:
For each angle, the design gap height is the 95% quantile of the AMD1 log-normal distribution, and the shell stiffness is interpolated for that angle:

from pyflange.flangesegments import PolynomialLFlangeSegment, Gap, shell_stiffness
from pyflange.stats import gap_height_distribution

print("AMD1: design gap = 95% quantile of the log-normal distribution")
amd1_damage = {}
for angle_deg in (30, 60, 90, 120):
    angle = angle_deg * deg
    k_design = gap_height_distribution(D, u_tol, angle * D/2).ppf(0.95)
    fseg = PolynomialLFlangeSegment(**common,
                                    gap = Gap(height=k_design, angle=angle),
                                    k_shell = shell_stiffness(R, s, angle))
    amd1_damage[angle_deg] = BoltFatigueAnalysis(fseg, mkvm).damage
    print(f"  gap angle {angle_deg:3d} deg   gap height {k_design/mm:4.2f} mm   damage {amd1_damage[angle_deg]:.3f}")

governing = max(amd1_damage, key=amd1_damage.get)
print(f"  governing gap angle: {governing} deg")

AMD1: design gap = 95% quantile of the log-normal distribution
  gap angle  30 deg   gap height 0.89 mm   damage 0.558
  gap angle  60 deg   gap height 1.68 mm   damage 0.869
  gap angle  90 deg   gap height 2.75 mm   damage 1.337
  gap angle 120 deg   gap height 4.12 mm   damage 1.231
  governing gap angle: 90 deg

The design gap heights match Table 2 of ref. [1]. The 30° gap of the L-flange tutorial is not the governing one: with a 90° gap the damage exceeds 1.0 and the flange fails the check.

docs.title: 3. ED2
docs.text:
The model proposed for ED2 (ref. [5], 9.7) changes the gap stiffness, the gap closing force (torsional correction) and the lower bound of the parameter a*. The ED2 design gap height is the 75% quantile of a Weibull distribution (ref. [5], 2.2.4):

from pyflange.flangesegments import PolynomialLFlangeSegmentED2
from pyflange.stats import gap_height_distribution_ED2

print("ED2: design gap = 75% quantile of the Weibull distribution")
for angle_deg in (30, 60, 90, 120):
    angle = angle_deg * deg
    k_design = gap_height_distribution_ED2(D, u_tol, angle * D/2).ppf(0.75)
    fseg = PolynomialLFlangeSegmentED2(**common,
                                       gap = Gap(height=k_design, angle=angle),
                                       k_shell = shell_stiffness(R, s, angle))
    damage = BoltFatigueAnalysis(fseg, mkvm).damage
    print(f"  gap angle {angle_deg:3d} deg   gap height {k_design/mm:4.2f} mm   damage {damage:.3f}")

ED2: design gap = 75% quantile of the Weibull distribution
  gap angle  30 deg   gap height 0.57 mm   damage 0.418
  gap angle  60 deg   gap height 1.27 mm   damage 0.569
  gap angle  90 deg   gap height 2.16 mm   damage 0.760
  gap angle 120 deg   gap height 3.25 mm   damage 0.736

With the smaller ED2 design gaps the same flange passes. Note that the ED2 design gap fractile was selected together with the partial safety factors (ref. [5], 6.7), so a lower damage does not simply mean that ED2 is less conservative.

Warning

The ED2 classes follow the draft background document of 2026-08-04 (ref. [5]) and may change before ED2 is published.

docs.title: Running the same study from the command line
docs.text:
The determ command accepts --gap-angle and --gap-height:

py -m pyflange determ case.json --gap-angle 90 --gap-height 2.75

When the gap angle is changed, the shell stiffness is interpolated again for the new angle. See the command line page and Writing case files from Python for batches.

docs.title: L-flange, deterministic analysis
docs.text:
This tutorial performs the deterministic bolt fatigue assessment of an L-flange according to IEC 61400-6 AMD1, for a single design gap. It covers the whole chain: bolt, gap, flange segment, validity check, bolt force and moment curves, fatigue damage.

Download the full script: lflange.py. Run it with py lflange.py.

docs.title: 1. Units
docs.text:
PyFlange works with any consistent system of units. We use SI units and define a few factors to make the input readable:

from math import pi

mm  = 0.001     # m
kN  = 1000      # N
MPa = 1e6       # Pa
deg = pi/180    # rad

docs.title: 2. Bolt, nut and bolt hole
docs.text:
from pyflange.bolts import StandardMetricBolt, RoundNut, standard_hole_diameter

bolt = StandardMetricBolt("M80", "10.9",
                          shank_length = 160*mm,
                          shank_diameter_ratio = "pitch",   # reduced shank
                          stud = True)
nut = RoundNut("M80")
Do = standard_hole_diameter("M80")      # 86 mm bolt hole
  • StandardMetricBolt creates a bolt with ISO thread dimensions and the properties of the material grade. stud=True models a stud bolt with two nuts; shank_diameter_ratio="pitch" gives a reduced shank with the diameter of the thread pitch diameter.
  • RoundNut is a flanged round nut. Use ISOHexNut for a hexagon nut, and pass a ISOFlatWasher as washer if there is one.
  • standard_hole_diameter returns the standard clearance hole.

docs.title: 3. Design gap
docs.text:
The polynomial model accounts for a gap between the two flanges, caused by flatness imperfections. IEC 61400-6 AMD1 defines the design gap height as the 95% quantile of a log-normal distribution that depends on the tower diameter, the flatness tolerance and the gap length (ref. [2], 6.7.5.2):

from pyflange.stats import gap_height_distribution
from pyflange.flangesegments import Gap, shell_stiffness

D = 8000*mm                 # flange (tower) outer diameter
u_tol = 1.4*mm / 1.0        # flatness tolerance: 1.4 mm/m
gap_angle = 30*deg          # gap angle
gap_length = gap_angle * D/2

gap_dist = gap_height_distribution(D, u_tol, gap_length)
gap = Gap(height = gap_dist.ppf(0.95),   # design gap: 95% quantile
          angle = gap_angle)

For an 8 m tower with a 1.4 mm/m tolerance and a 30° gap, the design gap height is 0.89 mm. In this tutorial we check the 30° gap only. The standard requires the gap angles 30°, 60°, 90° and 120°: see Design gap angles and ED2.

docs.title: 4. Flange segment
docs.text:
The model describes one segment of the flange: the slice that contains one bolt (see Model overview and Nomenclature for the symbols).

L-flange segment: cross-section with the parameters a, b, s, t, R, Do and the shell force Z Z Z a b t t s Do R (outer radius) shell flange bolt ← tower axis (inside) outside → 
from pyflange.flangesegments import PolynomialLFlangeSegment

n_bolts = 156               # number of bolts in the flange
R = D/2                     # shell outer radius
s = 54*mm                   # shell thickness

fseg = PolynomialLFlangeSegment(
    a = 150*mm,             # inner face of the flange to bolt axis
    b = 122*mm,             # bolt axis to shell center line
    s = s,
    t = 172*mm,             # flange thickness
    R = R,
    central_angle = 2*pi / n_bolts,

    Zg = -18044*kN / n_bolts,           # dead weight per bolt (compression)

    bolt = bolt,
    Fv = 2876*kN,                       # bolt preload before losses
    Do = Do,
    washer = None,
    nut = nut,

    gap = gap,
    tilt_angle = 0.1*deg,               # inside flange inclination

    k_shell = shell_stiffness(R, s, gap_angle),   # shell stiffness from FEA data
    PPL = 0.05,                         # 5% preload loss due to plastic strain
    DFT = 300e-6,                       # 300 um coating thickness
    settlement_factor = 0.5)            # tension tightening with re-tightening

Some parameters deserve attention:

  • Zg is the shell force per bolt in the unloaded state, normally the dead weight above the flange divided by the number of bolts. It is negative because it compresses the flange.
  • Fv is the preload before losses. The losses due to settlement (DFT, settlement_factor, ref. [2], eqs. (27) and (28)) and plastic strain (PPL, ref. [2], eq. (24)) are subtracted by the model. The resulting preload is available as fseg.bolt_preload. If your Fv already includes all losses, leave PPL and DFT at their default value of zero.
  • k_shell is the shell stiffness. Here it is interpolated from a database of FEA results with shell_stiffness. If omitted, the simplified formula of ref. [2], eq. G.43 is used, which is conservative.
  • tilt_angle is the inclination of the flange contact surface. A positive value (inclination towards the inside) reduces the bolt forces.
  • E, G, s_ratio (bottom shell thickness over s) and r (fillet radius) have default values; see PolynomialLFlangeSegment.

docs.title: 5. Check that the model is applicable
docs.text:
The polynomial model of an L-flange is valid only if failure mode B (plastic hinges in the flange and in the shell) is the governing ultimate failure mode (ref. [2], eq. G.30):

mode, Zu = fseg.failure_mode(fy_sh=355*MPa, fy_fl=335*MPa)
print(f"Governing failure mode: {mode}")
print(f"Ultimate shell forces A, B, D, E [kN]: {[round(Z/kN) for Z in Zu]}")

fseg.validate(fy_sh=355*MPa, fy_fl=335*MPa)    # raises ValueError if mode B does not govern

Governing failure mode: B
Ultimate shell forces A, B, D, E [kN]: [3128, 1805, 2206, 5503]

validate() raises a ValueError if another mode governs, so a script stops before producing results outside the validity range of the model.

docs.title: 6. Bolt force curve
docs.text:
The bolt force curve is defined by four points (ref. [2], Table G.1):

print(f"Preload after losses: {fseg.bolt_preload/kN:.0f} kN")
print(f"P1 (at rest):       Z = {fseg.shell_force_at_rest/kN:8.1f} kN   Fs = {fseg.bolt_force_at_rest/kN:7.1f} kN")
print(f"P2 (tensile ULS):   Z = {fseg.shell_force_at_tensile_ULS/kN:8.1f} kN   Fs = {fseg.bolt_force_at_tensile_ULS/kN:7.1f} kN")
print(f"P3 (small displ.):  Z = {fseg.shell_force_at_small_displacement/kN:8.1f} kN   Fs = {fseg.bolt_force_at_small_displacement/kN:7.1f} kN")
print(f"P4 (gap closed):    Z = {fseg.shell_force_at_closed_gap/kN:8.1f} kN")

Preload after losses: 2669 kN
P1 (at rest):       Z =   -115.7 kN   Fs =  2669.2 kN
P2 (tensile ULS):   Z =   1840.0 kN   Fs =  3336.6 kN
P3 (small displ.):  Z =    111.1 kN   Fs =  2677.0 kN
P4 (gap closed):    Z =   -427.5 kN

The transfer functions accept a single value or a numpy array of shell forces:

import numpy as np

Z = np.linspace(-500*kN, 1500*kN, 201)     # shell force per bolt
Fs = fseg.bolt_axial_force(Z)              # bolt axial force
Ms = fseg.bolt_bending_moment(Z)           # bolt bending moment

print(f"Fs(Z = 500 kN) = {fseg.bolt_axial_force(500*kN)/kN:.1f} kN")
print(f"Ms(Z = 500 kN) = {fseg.bolt_bending_moment(500*kN)/1000:.2f} kNm")

With matplotlib installed, the script also plots the curves:

try:
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
except ImportError:
    plt = None      # matplotlib is optional: py -m pip install matplotlib

if plt:
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
    ax1.plot(Z/kN, Fs/kN)
    ax1.set_xlabel("Shell force Z [kN]")
    ax1.set_ylabel("Bolt axial force Fs [kN]")
    ax1.grid(True)
    ax2.plot(Z/kN, Ms/1000)
    ax2.set_xlabel("Shell force Z [kN]")
    ax2.set_ylabel("Bolt bending moment Ms [kNm]")
    ax2.grid(True)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("lflange-transfer-functions.png")

Below P1 the flange is compressed and the gap closes: at P4 it is completely closed and the bolt force stays constant. Above P1 the bolt force increases quadratically up to the ultimate state P2. P3 sets the initial slope of the curve.

docs.title: 7. Fatigue analysis
docs.text:
The fatigue loads are given as a Markov matrix of tower bending moments at the flange. BoltFatigueAnalysis converts them into bolt stresses through the transfer functions and computes the damage with the IEC bolt S-N curve (detail category 50, size effect, γM = 1.1, ref. [2], 6.7.5.4):

from pyflange.fatigue import MarkovMatrix, BoltFatigueAnalysis

# Tower bending moment Markov matrix at the flange, for 30 years
mkvm = MarkovMatrix(
    range  = np.array([ 25,  50, 100, 150, 200, 250,  300, 375, 500, 625]) * 1e6,   # N·m
    mean   = np.array([100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 100,  100, 100, 100, 100]) * 1e6,   # N·m
    cycles = np.array([3e8, 1e8, 3e7, 8e6, 2e6, 5e5, 1.5e5, 4e4, 8e3, 1e3]),
    duration = 30)                                                                 # years

fatigue = BoltFatigueAnalysis(fseg, mkvm)

print(f"S-N curve knee point: {fatigue.fatigue_curve.curves[0].DS_ref/MPa:.1f} MPa")
print(f"Damage:       {fatigue.damage:.3f}")
print(f"Fatigue life: {fatigue.fatigue_life:.1f} years")

S-N curve knee point: 40.1 MPa
Damage:       0.558
Fatigue life: 53.8 years

The damage is below 1.0, so the bolts pass for the 30° gap. The bolt stress Markov matrix is available as fatigue.bolt_mkvm, and a different S-N curve can be passed as custom_fatigue_curve. A stress multiplication factor (SMF) can be applied to the bolt stress ranges.

docs.title: Monte Carlo from the command line
docs.text:
A deterministic analysis uses design values for every input. A Monte Carlo simulation instead draws many random realizations of the uncertain inputs (preload, gap, inclination, loads, S-N curve, Miner's rule), computes the damage of each one and gives the statistical distribution of the results, for example to estimate a probability of failure. This is the approach used to calibrate the safety factors of IEC 61400-6 (refs. [1] and [5], section 6).

This tutorial runs a Monte Carlo simulation with the pyflange command line, without writing code.

docs.title: 1. The case file
docs.text:
Use the example case fatigue-case.json from Getting started. Besides the deterministic data, it contains a Stats section with the random variables:

"Stats": {
    "Preload":            { "Distribution": "Normal", "MeanRatio": 0.77, "CoV": 0.03 },
    "PlasticLoss":        { "Distribution": "Normal", "Mean": 0.03, "CoV": 0.33333 },
    "DFT":                { "Distribution": "Normal", "Mean": 250e-6, "CoV": 0.12 },
    "Gap": {
        "JointDistribution": "IEC 61400-6:2020 AMD1",
        "FlatnessTolerance": 0.0014,
        "Angle":       { "Distribution": "LogNormal", "Mean": 1.745, "CoV": 1.0 },
        "ShapeFactor": { "Distribution": "Normal", "Mean": 1.0, "CoV": 0.15 }
    },
    "Tilt":               { "Distribution": "LogNormal", "Mean": 0.001745, "CoV": 0.5 },
    "LoadRangeFactor":    { "Distribution": "LogNormal", "Mean": 1.0, "CoV": 0.12 },
    "FatigueClassFactor": { "Distribution": "Normal", "Mean": 1.0, "CoV": 0.10, "DS_ref_mean": 62e6 },
    "AllowableDamage":    { "Distribution": "LogNormal", "Mean": 1.0, "CoV": 0.30 },
    "StressMultiplicationFactor": { ... }
}

The values follow the stochastic model of ref. [5], Table 8. Each key is described in the JSON format reference, which also explains how a realization is generated.

docs.title: 2. Generate the sample
docs.text:
C:\Users\yourname\flange-analyses>py -m pyflange sample fatigue-case.json --size 2000 --seed 1
Performing probabilistic analysis for case fatigue-case.json ...
... loading data from 'C:\Users\yourname\flange-analyses\fatigue-case.json'
... generating random sample of 2000 realizations with seed 1
... ... generated 1000 realizations
... ... generated 2000 realizations
... writing results to file '.\fatigue-case-sample.csv'
... DONE!
  • --size is the number of realizations. 2000 takes about 15 seconds. For an estimate of a probability of failure of 10-4 you need well over 105 realizations (the default is 100 000).
  • --seed makes the simulation reproducible: the same seed and case always give the same sample. Without it, every run is different.
  • --xlsx also writes the sample to an Excel file.

The CSV file has one row per realization, numbered from 0, with the random inputs and the results (Damage, AllowableDamage, FatigueLife, Utilization = damage / allowable damage). The columns are listed on the command line page.

docs.title: 3. Statistics
docs.text:

docs.title: Monte Carlo in Python
docs.text:
This tutorial builds a Monte Carlo simulation of the bolt fatigue damage with the random samplers of pyflange.stats. It does the same as the sample command, but in a script, so you can change any distribution, add random variables, or post-process the results as you like.

Download the full script: montecarlo.py

docs.title: Samplers
docs.text:
A sampler is a Python generator: an object that returns a new random value every time you call next() on it.

from pyflange.stats import norm_sampler

preload = norm_sampler(2876e3, 0.03)    # normal, mean 2876 kN, CoV 3%
next(preload)                           # a random preload, e.g. 2.91e6
next(preload)                           # another one, e.g. 2.84e6

PyFlange has generic samplers (norm_sampler, lognorm_sampler, weibull_sampler, beta_sampler, sampler for any scipy distribution) and samplers of PyFlange objects, which combine other samplers:

Sampler Yields standard_gap_sampler Random Gap (AMD1 gap height distribution) standard_gap_sampler_ED2 Random Gap (ED2 distributions) standard_PolynomialLFlangeSegment_sampler Random L-flange segments standard_markov_matrix_sampler Markov matrices with random load ranges standard_bolt_fatigue_curve_sampler Random bolt S-N curves fatigue_case_sampler Random BoltFatigueAnalysis objects

You can write your own samplers too: any generator that yields objects of the right type works.

docs.title: 1. Reproducibility
docs.text:
The samplers use the global numpy random generator. Seed it to get the same sample at every run:

np.random.seed(1)       # makes the simulation reproducible

docs.title: 2. Flange segment sampler
docs.text:
import pyflange.stats as stats
from pyflange.bolts import StandardMetricBolt, RoundNut, standard_hole_diameter

D = 8000*mm
n_bolts = 156
bolt = StandardMetricBolt("M80", "10.9", shank_length=160*mm,
                          shank_diameter_ratio="pitch", stud=True)

fseg_sampler = stats.standard_PolynomialLFlangeSegment_sampler(
    a = 150*mm, b = 122*mm, s = 54*mm, t = 172*mm, R = D/2,
    central_angle = 2*pi / n_bolts,
    Zg = -18044*kN / n_bolts,
    bolt = bolt,
    Do = standard_hole_diameter("M80"),
    washer = None,
    nut = RoundNut("M80"),

    # Random preload before losses: mean 2876 kN, CoV 3%
    preload_sampler = stats.norm_sampler(2876*kN, 0.03),

    # Random preload losses (ref. [5], section 6.4.1)
    ppl_sampler = stats.norm_sampler(0.03, 1/3),        # plastic loss: mean 3%, std 1%
    dft_sampler = stats.norm_sampler(250*um, 0.12),     # coating: mean 250 um, std 30 um

    # Random gap: AMD1 gap height distribution with random angle and shape
    gap_sampler = stats.standard_gap_sampler(
        flange_diameter = D,
        flange_flatness_tolerance = 0.0014,
        gap_angle_sampler = stats.lognorm_sampler(100*deg, 1.0),
        gap_shape_factor_sampler = stats.norm_sampler(1.0, 0.15)),

    # Random inside flange inclination: LN(0.1 deg, CoV 0.5)
    tilt_sampler = stats.lognorm_sampler(0.1*deg, 0.5),

    settlement_factor = 0.5)

For each realization, the sampler draws a gap and a flange inclination, then draws the preload and its losses for half of the bolts within the gap and averages them (ref. [5], 4.4). The yielded segment has the averaged preload after losses as Fv, and PPL = DFT = 0.

The distributions are those of the stochastic model of ref. [5], Table 8, except the gap angle, which the reference does not give.

docs.title: 3. Loads, S-N curve and Miner's rule
docs.text:
from pyflange.fatigue import MarkovMatrix

design_mkvm = MarkovMatrix(
    range  = np.array([ 25,  50, 100, 150, 200, 250,  300, 375, 500, 625]) * 1e6,
    mean   = np.array([100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 100,  100, 100, 100, 100]) * 1e6,
    cycles = np.array([3e8, 1e8, 3e7, 8e6, 2e6, 5e5, 1.5e5, 4e4, 8e3, 1e3]),
    duration = 30)

# Load ranges scaled by X_FLS ~ LN(1.0, 0.12)
mkvm_sampler = stats.standard_markov_matrix_sampler(design_mkvm, 1.0, 0.12)

# Bolt S-N curve with DS_ref = X_FAT ~ N(62 MPa, 0.10)
sn_sampler = stats.standard_bolt_fatigue_curve_sampler(bolt.nominal_diameter, 1.0, 0.10, 62*MPa)

# Miner's rule uncertainty: allowable damage ~ LN(1.0, 0.30)
allowable_damage_sampler = stats.lognorm_sampler(1.0, 0.30)

docs.title: 4. Fatigue case sampler
docs.text:
The four samplers are combined into a sampler of complete fatigue analyses:

fcase_sampler = stats.fatigue_case_sampler(fseg_sampler,
                                           mkvm_sampler,
                                           sn_sampler,
                                           allowable_damage_sampler)

fcase = next(fcase_sampler)         # one random BoltFatigueAnalysis
print(f"One realization: gap angle {fcase.fseg.gap.angle/deg:.0f} deg, "
      f"gap height {fcase.fseg.gap.height/mm:.2f} mm, damage {fcase.damage:.3g}")

One realization: gap angle 46 deg, gap height 0.19 mm, damage 0.0397

Each realization is a BoltFatigueAnalysis: fcase.fseg is the random segment, fcase.flange_mkvm the random Markov matrix, fcase.fatigue_curve the random S-N curve, fcase.allowable_damage the random allowable damage, and fcase.damage and fcase.fatigue_life the results.

docs.title: 5. Generate the sample
docs.text:
Collect the values of interest in a pandas table:

import pandas as pd

rows = []
for i in range(SAMPLE_SIZE):
    fcase = next(fcase_sampler)
    rows.append({
        "GapAngle":        fcase.fseg.gap.angle,
        "GapHeight":       fcase.fseg.gap.height,
        "BoltPreload":     fcase.fseg.bolt_preload,
        "Damage":          fcase.damage,
        "AllowableDamage": fcase.allowable_damage,
        "FatigueLife":     fcase.fatigue_life,
    })
    if (i+1) % 500 == 0:
        print(f"... {i+1} realizations")

sample = pd.DataFrame(rows)

This tutorial repeats the L-flange tutorial for a T-flange and highlights the differences. Read the L-flange tutorial first.

docs.text: L-flange T-flange Class PolynomialLFlangeSegment PolynomialTFlangeSegment Bolts per segment 1 2 (one on each side of the shell) central_angle 2π / number of bolts 2π / number of bolt pairs Zg Dead weight per bolt Dead weight per bolt pair a Inner face of the flange to bolt axis Edge of the flange to bolt axis tilt_angle Optional (default 0) Required: IEC 61400-6 requires the flange taper to be always considered (ref. [2], G.2.4) Governing failure mode for the model to be valid B A (ref. [2], eq. G.31) Tensile bolt moment Quadratic in Z Cubic in Z (ref. [2], eq. docs.title: 1. Flange segment
docs.text:
T-flange segment: cross-section with the parameters a, b, s, t, R, Do and the shell force Z Z Z a b b a t t s Do R (outer radius) shell flange flange ← tower axis (inside) outside → 
from pyflange.bolts import StandardMetricBolt, ISOHexNut, standard_hole_diameter
from pyflange.flangesegments import PolynomialTFlangeSegment, Gap, shell_stiffness
from pyflange.stats import gap_height_distribution

D = 7500*mm                 # tower outer diameter
n_pairs = 200               # number of bolt pairs (one inside and one outside the shell)
s = 90*mm                   # shell thickness

gap_angle = 30*deg
gap_dist = gap_height_distribution(D, 0.0014, gap_angle * D/2)

fseg = PolynomialTFlangeSegment(
    a = 62.5*mm,            # flange edge to bolt axis
    b = 111*mm,             # bolt axis to shell center line
    s = s,
    t = 120*mm,             # flange thickness
    R = D/2,                # shell outer radius
    central_angle = 2*pi / n_pairs,

    Zg = -105.8*kN,         # dead weight per bolt pair (compression)

    bolt = StandardMetricBolt("M48", "10.9", shank_length=150*mm,
                              shank_diameter_ratio="pitch", stud=True),
    Fv = 928*kN,            # preload of each bolt, before losses
    Do = standard_hole_diameter("M48"),
    washer = None,
    nut = ISOHexNut("M48"),

    gap = Gap(height = gap_dist.ppf(0.95), angle = gap_angle),
    tilt_angle = 0.0,       # required: no taper effect for this flange

    k_shell = shell_stiffness(D/2, s, gap_angle))

The bolt force Fs and moment Ms returned by the model are those of one bolt of the pair, for the shell force Z acting on the whole segment.

tilt_angle = 0.0 is allowed only if the taper of the flange ensures that the first contact point is directly below the tower wall (ref. [2], 6.7.5.3). Otherwise, use the worst-case inclination allowed by the manufacturing specification.

docs.title: 4. Fatigue analysis
docs.text:
The fatigue analysis is the same as for the L-flange:

from pyflange.fatigue import MarkovMatrix, BoltFatigueAnalysis

mkvm = MarkovMatrix(
    range  = np.array([ 20,  40,  80, 120, 160, 200, 240, 300, 400, 500]) * 1e6,   # N·m
    mean   = np.array([ 80,  80,  80,  80,  80,  80,  80,  80,  80,  80]) * 1e6,   # N·m
    cycles = np.array([3e8, 1e8, 3e7, 8e6, 2e6, 5e5, 1.5e5, 4e4, 8e3, 1e3]),
    duration = 25)                                                               # years

fatigue = BoltFatigueAnalysis(fseg, mkvm)
print(f"Damage:       {fatigue.damage:.3f}")
print(f"Fatigue life: {fatigue.fatigue_life:.0f} years")

Damage:       0.667
Fatigue life: 38 years
